title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 125 (Rights of indemnity-holder when sued)

content.overview: Section 125 provides that the promisee in a contract of indemnity, acting within the scope of his authority, is entitled to recover from the promisor: (1) all damages which he may be compelled to pay in any suit in respect of any matter to which the promise to indemnify applies; (2) all costs which he may be compelled to pay in any such suit if, in bringing or defending it, he did not contravene the orders of the promisor, and acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity, or if the promisor authorised him to bring or defend the suit; (3) all sums which he may have paid under the terms of any compromise of any such suit, if the compromise was not contrary to the orders of the promisor, and was one which it would have been prudent for the promisee to make in the absence of any contract of indemnity, or if the promisor authorised him to compromise the suit.
content.glance: Indemnity-holder acting within authority may recover damages in covered suits, qualifying costs, and qualifying compromise sums from the promisor.
content.study: The promisee (indemnity-holder) in a contract of indemnity, acting within the scope of his authority, is entitled to recover from the promisor three heads: (1) all damages compelled to be paid in any suit relating to a matter covered by the indemnity; (2) all costs compelled to be paid in such a suit, provided he did not contravene the promisor’s orders and acted as a prudent person would have acted without an indemnity, or the promisor authorised the suit; (3) all sums paid under a compromise of such a suit, provided the compromise was not contrary to the promisor’s orders and was one a prudent person would have made without an indemnity, or the promisor authorised the compromise. Current-law framing: confirm indemnity under s. 124; confirm action within authority; identify the head of recovery and test the statutory conditions for costs or compromise.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.body: All damages which he may be compelled to pay in any suit in respect of any matter to which the promise to indemnify applies.

sections.heading: Costs
sections.body: All costs which he may be compelled to pay in any such suit if, in bringing or defending it, he did not contravene the orders of the promisor, and acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity, or if the promisor authorised him to bring or defend the suit.

sections.heading: Compromise sums
sections.body: All sums which he may have paid under the terms of any compromise of any such suit, if the compromise was not contrary to the orders of the promisor, and was one which it would have been prudent for the promisee to make in the absence of any contract of indemnity, or if the promisor authorised him to compromise the suit.

examples.title: Recovery of damages
examples.body: An indemnity-holder, acting within authority, is compelled to pay damages in a suit covering a matter to which the indemnity applies and recovers those damages from the promisor under s. 125(1).

examples.title: Qualifying costs
examples.body: Costs are recoverable where the indemnity-holder did not contravene the promisor’s orders and acted prudently, or was authorised to bring or defend the suit.

hypotheticals.question: Can an indemnity-holder recover a compromise payment made against the promisor’s express orders?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 125(3) requires that the compromise not be contrary to the orders of the promisor (or that the promisor authorised it).

misconceptions.trap: All costs and all compromise payments are automatically recoverable.
misconceptions.correction: Costs and compromise sums are recoverable only if the statutory conditions (no contravention of orders + prudence, or authorisation) are met.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 125 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Confirm a contract of indemnity and action within authority. II. Identify the head (damages, costs or compromise). III. For costs or compromise, test the statutory conditions. IV. Conclude.
